newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Mar 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Mar 27.

text.p: New Zealand has been labelled a "small but briliant star" for its 10th place in the Geneva-based world competitiveness league. Based on 63 percent of the data processed for the 46 nations ranked in the IMD World Competitiveness Yearbook, New Zealand is up a point on last year, ahead of such heavyweights as Japan, U.K., Germany, Australia, South Korea, Sweden, France and Taiwan. The country's performance has been remarkably consistent since is soared to 10th place in the league in 1994. In 1995, it was ninth and last year, 11th. Page 1.

A determined government push behind the compulsory superannuation scheme proposal could yet see it succeed in the September referendum. While most polling has come out against a compulsory scheme, the latest National Business Review-Consultus poll shows a majority in favour of a scheme in principle. But when questioned further, a majority is against having to save up to eight percent of income to fund retirement. Page 1.

A Commerce Ministry says it has no records of a three-month period when one of its senior officials was deeply involved in the setting-up of the pilot Maori television, ATN. The official, who has since been moved to another part of the ministry, was involved in numerous contacts with the Maori funding agency, Te Mangai Paho, during the establishment of the station. Page 1.

Fisheries Minister John Luxton's shutdown of the Auckland Islands squid fishery in the Southern Ocean will cost fishing companies up to $20 million. The industry, worth between $120 million and $160 million in exports a year, was closed because 102 of the 13,500 Hooker sea lions were accidentally caught in squid nets. Luxton said he was reluctant to close the fishery but had to by law after it was discovered more than the allowed 73 mammals had been caught and died. Page 2.

The publishers of the venerable Rugby News and upstart NZ Rugby Monthly are locked in a maul over a new title launched this month. The ruckus started after Front Row Publishing pulled out of a deal to buy into Rugby News at the last minute. A joint-venture deal between the two companies had gone as far as office rental and production agreements. Then, just beofore the final agreements were to be signed, Front Row backed out and launched its own monthly magazine. Page 4.

Inland Revenue is misinterpreting court rulings in its treatment of the All Blacks' tax status. Its use of a checklist process has been superseded by those rulings, an industrial law paper has found. By applying the tests from the relevant court decisions, master of the laws student Marcus Wells finds the All Blacks and other elite rugby players now under contract to All Blacks Promotions are independent contractors for tax purposes. Page 5.

Chrysler Corporation boss Bob Eaton predicts as many as one in four new vehicles will be sold via the Internet in five years. Eaton, who is chairman, president and chief executive of the American motor company giant, believes car buyers are unhappy with the current haggling of new car buying and want a more transparent system. Tomorrow's buyer won't be "walking out (of a dealer showroom) wondering if he got screwed," Eaton said during his Down Under tour. Page 8.

The coalition is planning a massive overhaul of employment law. However, the move could test its resolve to present a united front. Labour Minister Max Bradford has several concernes about the current employment framework. he believes there have been a raft of Employment Court decisions inconsistent with the principles of the act. These, combined with similar decisions made by the Employment Tribunal, could be "adversely affecting employment prospects and flexibility in the labour market," he told a seminar in Wellington last week. Page 9.

The Rugby Union has rejected a proposal to tender top test matches to the highest cash bidders, opting instead to continue playing the major tests in the four main centres. Chief executive David Moffet said staging category A tests with key rugby nations in Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch and Dunedin was part of the union's determination to "promote the game". "It would be unfair not to take a category A test to Dunedin becuase it couldn't match the fee amont from, say, Auckland," he said. Page 10.

Shares in southern entrepreneur Howard Paterson's recently cancelled public deer float have been placed with a handful of private investors who will pay up today. The plans to publicly list the shares of New Zealand Deer Farms and form the largest farmed deer herd in the country were shelved last month because, brokers said, the offering failed to enthuse investors. But while it may have failed to excite a wide range of investors, Paterson this week said a private offering for shares in the company, arranged by organising broker First NZ Capital had identified the interested investors. Page 10.

New Zealand, British and Dutch partners are close to launching a new shipping consortium to dominate the increasingly competitive transtasman trade. The alliance, between Auckland-based Tasman Express Line, South Pacific Shipping of Christchurch and multinational giant P&O Nedlloyd, was expected to be announced today. SPS managing director Captain Ross Fast said negotiations which began more than a month ago were close to completion. Page 11.

Ostrich meat is being supplied to a Christchurch hotel by a group of Canterbury ostrich farmers in an effort to lend creditibility to the industry. Trading as Canterbury Ostrich Processors, the group made their debut at the Chateau on the Park restaurant a couple of weeks ago. It was the same week the Commerce Commission banned advertisements by the Savannah Ostrich Processing Company NZ for failing to comply with the Securities Act. Page 11.
